title: Industrial Property Identification
name: Industrial Property Identification
metaTitle: Industrial Property Identification in Fort Worth, TX
metaDescription: Fort Worth industrial 1031 exchange identification: sourcing rail-served and air-cargo replacement buildings near AllianceTexas within the 45-day window.

sections.html: Identifying an industrial replacement property within the 45-day window requires more upfront homework than a straightforward retail or office trade, since building specifications, rail or highway access, and clear-height requirements vary widely across submarkets. Fort Worth investors exchanging into industrial product frequently look toward the AllianceTexas inland port, where BNSF intermodal rail and air-cargo infrastructure support a distinct set of building types.

sections.heading: Reading the Alliance Corridor
sections.html:
The Alliance area's mix of bulk distribution, rail-served, and air-cargo-adjacent buildings means two properties listed at similar price points can serve very different tenant profiles. A rail-served building near the BNSF intermodal facility supports different lease economics than a smaller flex-industrial property closer to Haslet or Saginaw, so identification screening starts with building specifications rather than price per square foot alone.

Clear height, dock door count, trailer parking, and rail spur access are the specifications that determine whether a candidate building actually functions as a replacement for the relinquished asset's tenant base, rather than simply falling into the same broad industrial category.

sections.heading: Screening Candidates Against the 45-Day Deadline
sections.html:
Because the identification window is fixed regardless of how quickly industrial product moves, candidate screening starts with brokers and listing services before the relinquished sale closes, so a short list already exists on day one. Bulk buildings near Alliance with strong BNSF access tend to draw competing offers quickly, which narrows the realistic candidate pool fast once a property comes to market.

  • Confirm clear height and dock door count against tenant requirements
  • Verify rail spur or highway access relevant to the tenant base
  • Check zoning and any air-cargo-adjacent use restrictions near Alliance
  • Assess environmental Phase I status before including a candidate on the list

sections.heading: Environmental and Title Considerations
sections.html: Industrial parcels, particularly older buildings or sites with prior manufacturing use, often carry Phase I environmental review requirements that take longer than a typical office or retail title search. Building that lead time into the identification and due diligence schedule prevents an otherwise qualifying candidate from being dropped late in the window over an unresolved environmental question.

sections.heading: Balancing Alliance Against Other Fort Worth Industrial Nodes
sections.html: While Alliance draws significant attention for its rail and air-cargo access, smaller industrial nodes near Crowley, Burleson, and White Settlement offer replacement candidates with lower price points and different tenant profiles, which broadens the identification list when the relinquished sale value does not support Alliance-area pricing.

sections.heading: Coordinating Broker Outreach Across Multiple Industrial Corridors
sections.html:
Because industrial listings move quickly once they hit the market, particularly near the AllianceTexas inland port, identification work benefits from standing broker relationships across several corridors rather than a single point of contact covering only one submarket. A broker with strong Alliance coverage may not have the same visibility into smaller, off-market opportunities near Saginaw or Haslet, so a coordinated search typically draws on more than one relationship simultaneously.

That parallel outreach is set up before the relinquished sale closes whenever possible, so the identification team is not starting broker conversations from scratch once the 45-day clock has already begun.

A standing list of active and recently closed industrial listings across the Alliance, Saginaw, Haslet, and Crowley areas, refreshed regularly rather than pulled together only when a search begins, shortens the time needed to build a credible candidate list once a relinquished sale is under contract. That preparation is what allows an identification team to move from a blank list to a defensible set of candidates within the first two weeks of the 45-day window rather than the last two. Keeping notes on which buildings were considered and ruled out, along with the reason, also prevents the same unsuitable candidate from being re-evaluated later in the process when time pressure is higher. That same record, once the identification list is finalized, becomes useful again during due diligence, giving the team a quick reference for why a given building was prioritized over others that were reviewed and set aside. It also gives a lender or tax advisor reviewing the transaction later a clear sense of how the final candidate was selected. That written trail, kept consistently across every Fort Worth-area search regardless of asset type, becomes a reusable reference the next time an investor runs a similar identification process.

faqs.q: Why does the Alliance area matter for Fort Worth industrial exchanges?
faqs.a: The AllianceTexas inland port combines BNSF intermodal rail and air-cargo infrastructure, supporting industrial building types and lease structures that differ from smaller flex-industrial product elsewhere in the metro.

faqs.q: How much lead time does environmental review need before identification?
faqs.a: A Phase I environmental assessment can typically be ordered before the relinquished sale closes, giving results by the time a candidate needs to be added to the identification list, though older sites may require additional Phase II review.

faqs.q: What specifications matter most when screening an industrial replacement candidate?
faqs.a: Clear height, dock door count, trailer parking capacity, and rail or highway access are the specifications that determine whether a building actually functions for the intended tenant base.

faqs.q: Are smaller industrial nodes outside Alliance viable replacement candidates?
faqs.a: Yes. Areas such as Crowley, Burleson, and White Settlement offer industrial product at different price points and specifications, which can fit a smaller relinquished sale value better than Alliance-area pricing.

faqs.q: Can an industrial candidate be identified before its environmental review is complete?
faqs.a: Yes, identification only requires a specific address or legal description; environmental review can continue during the due diligence period before closing, though unresolved issues could affect the closing timeline.
